axes.model_access:
**The official docs give four paths and stress there is no lock-in.**

This is the most blunt statement of model freedom among everything we list.

**README original**:

"Use any model you want — **Nous Portal**, **OpenRouter, OpenAI, your own endpoint**, and many others. **Switch with `hermes model` — no code changes, no lock-in.**"

**The "your own endpoint" clause matters most to our readers.**
Self-built gateways and self-hosted inference connect directly.

**Switching models needs no code change — one runtime command**: `/model [provider:model]`.
The same command works in the CLI and on messaging platforms.
(See the CLI vs Messaging comparison table on the site.)

**The full provider list is verified**, from the official `docs/integrations/providers`.
The official docs list 40+ in total:

- Nous Portal — officially billed as "300+ frontier agentic models"
- OpenRouter, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot
- xAI Grok, Google Gemini / Vertex AI
- AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry
- DeepSeek, Hugging Face, NVIDIA Build
- Local / self-hosted: Ollama, LM Studio, and **Custom Endpoint**

For Custom Endpoint config the official docs say:

"saved in `config.yaml`"

**The official positioning of that page, verbatim**:

"from cloud APIs ... to self-hosted endpoints like **Ollama and vLLM**, to advanced routing and fallback configurations."

⚠ **Unknown: capability alignment after switching models, and behavior differences of local quantized models across backends — the official docs give no conclusion.**

We have not run measured tests either.

**Verified**: providers page and configuration page both checked.
axes.runtime:
**This is its strongest dimension: six terminal backends plus plugin backends, plus two entry points.**

**README original list** (2026-10-23 rolling-verification edition):

"**terminal backends** — **local, Docker, SSH, Modal, Daytona, and Vercel Sandbox** — **plus plugin backends such as Singularity/Apptainer**."

⚠ The older README (verified 2026-10-01) said "**Seven terminal backends** — local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, and Vercel Sandbox" —
**Singularity has since been moved by the official docs into plugin backends**; we record the current wording.

The official docs also single out two backends: Daytona and Modal.
They bring serverless persistence.

"your agent's environment **hibernates when idle and wakes on demand**, costing nearly nothing between sessions"

**There are two entry points.** The README has a dedicated CLI vs Messaging comparison table:

- Terminal TUI: launch `hermes`
- Messaging platforms: run the gateway first, then chat from Telegram / Discord / Slack / WhatsApp / Signal / Email, plus Home Assistant

⚠ **This is the most valuable cell on our site.** It is the only listed product that explicitly says "the agent can run on a cloud VM while you direct it from Telegram".

That is the same need as OpenHands' "the agent keeps running after you close the laptop".
The difference: OpenHands makes it an optional deployment, Hermes makes it the default form.
axes.local_files:
**Local-file capability comes indirectly: through terminal backends, not the framework itself.**

Isolation mechanisms are covered under the permissions axis.

**The workspace is determined by the chosen backend.** The official `terminal.backend` **defaults to `local`**.

**Official label, verbatim**: "Run on your machine (default)"

`terminal.backend` decides the workspace.
The working directory is decided by `cwd`.

Each backend provides one layer of isolation:

- Docker / SSH
- Modal / Daytona / Vercel
- Singularity (current README wording files it under plugin backends)

**Context Files are an official first-class concept; format and precedence verified.**
(docs `features/context-files`)
Supported filenames:

- `.hermes.md` / `HERMES.md`
- `AGENTS.md`, `AGENTS.override.md`
- `CLAUDE.md`
- `SOUL.md`
- `.cursorrules`, `.cursor/rules/*.mdc`

**Precedence is first match wins.** Order, verbatim:

`.hermes.md` → `AGENTS.override.md` → `AGENTS.md` → `CLAUDE.md` → `.cursorrules`.
`SOUL.md` is the identity file and is always loaded separately.

In a git repo, the whole `AGENTS.md` chain merges **git root → working directory**.
Subdirectory context is also discovered progressively during a session.
The per-file word cap is floor 20,000 / ceiling 500,000.

**File access has boundaries.** Layer 8 of the security page governs the terminal backend's working-directory parameter:

**Official wording**: "validated against an allowlist to prevent shell injection"

Layer 3 of the security page says `write_file` and `patch` have a denylist.
There is also an optional write sandbox.
axes.background:
**Its mechanism is thickest on this dimension: the official docs give three layers.**

**① Built-in cron scheduler.** Official feature-table wording:

"Built-in **cron scheduler** with delivery to any platform. Daily reports, nightly backups, weekly audits — all in natural language, **running unattended**."

(docs `features/cron`)

**② Serverless hibernate-and-wake.** Daytona / Modal / Vercel backends hibernate when idle and wake on demand; the official phrase is exactly these words:
**Official wording**: "hibernates when idle and wakes on demand"

**③ A resident gateway process.** Once the gateway runs, multiple messaging platforms can trigger it any time.

**Catch-up and re-run mechanics are officially documented** (`features/cron`):

- There is a **misfire catch-up** scan
- After `resume`, "the next tick fires one **catch-up run**"
- Catch-up can be disabled: `cron.catch_up_missed: false`
- While globally paused via `hermes pause`, the hosted cron's fire webhook returns `503 Retry-After: 60` so the scheduler re-delivers

- Officially: "nothing is lost: due work catches up on the first tick"
- Running tasks are "never killed"

The gateway side also has an **event-loop liveness watchdog**.
After 3 consecutive unresponsive probes it exits with code 75 and the supervisor restarts it.
There is also a 60s heartbeat.

⚠ **Unknown: state consistency across hibernate/wake — the official docs do not state it.**

**Verified**: `features/cron`, `features/tools`, `user-guide/messaging` — three pages checked.
axes.tools:
**The official docs say it has 40+ tools and explicitly support MCP.**

The docs directory has a dedicated "**Tools & Toolsets**" page, subtitle verbatim:

"**40+ tools**, toolset system, **terminal backends**"

(docs `features/tools`)

**MCP Integration is also its own docs page**, verbatim:

"Connect **any MCP server** for extended capabilities"

(docs `features/mcp`)

**One capability is quite unusual: subagent RPC.** Official wording:

"Spawn **isolated subagents** for parallel workstreams. **Write Python scripts that call tools via RPC**, collapsing multi-step pipelines into **zero-context-cost turns**."

⚠ **How we read "zero-context-cost":**
moving multi-step pipelines out of the context for execution —
i.e. only the result is returned to the context.
⚠ **The official docs give no concrete context-savings figure; we mark this as inference.**

The community also maintains an MCP server for controlling the Linux desktop,
named `computer-use-linux`.
It uses the AT-SPI accessibility tree + Wayland/X11 input + screenshots.

The README explicitly says it is for **"Hermes and other MCP hosts"**.
axes.context:
**⚠ This is the dimension our site cares about most, and also the one this product markets hardest — they must be kept apart.**

First, the official claims.

README feature table, the "A closed learning loop" row, verbatim:

"Agent-curated memory with **periodic nudges**. Autonomous skill creation after complex tasks. **Skills self-improve during use.** **FTS5 session search with LLM summarization for cross-session recall.** Honcho dialectic user modeling. Compatible with the agentskills.io open standard."

**But placing each official mechanism into its proper bucket shows this is not one dimension but three.**

| Official claim | Our categorization | Note |
|---|---|---|
| periodic nudges (self-prompting) | state plane | a mechanism trigger, not a compression algorithm |
| FTS5 session search + LLM summarization | **context plane ✅** | retrieval + summarization — **this is genuine context management** |
| Skills (autonomous creation + self-improvement during use) | its own layer | procedural memory, distinct from conversation context |
| Honcho dialectic user modeling | its own layer | long-term modeling of the user |

**Key distinction: compression is explicitly user-triggered.**
There is a dedicated `/compress` command,
in both the CLI and messaging platforms, listed alongside `/usage` and `/insights` in the comparison table.
That means: **no trigger, no compression** — it is not automatic.

**There is also a set of evidence that comes down to filenames.** From the "Migrating from OpenClaw" section,
an unusually concrete first-party official list:

- `SOUL.md` — persona
- `MEMORY.md` and `USER.md` — memory entries
- `AGENTS.md` — workspace instructions
- `~/.hermes/skills/openclaw-imports/` — skills directory

**This shows memory is plaintext markdown files — readable and portable.**
For our readers this is an important advantage.
axes.permissions:
**The official docs have a standalone "Security" section that splits the permissions surface into eight layers.**

**The eight layers, verbatim**:

- user authorization (allowlists, DM pairing)
- dangerous command approval
- file write safety
- container isolation
- MCP credential filtering
- context file scanning
- cross-session isolation
- input sanitization

Item-by-item verification (official `user-guide/security`):

**① Command approval (defaults verified).** `approvals.mode` has three settings, **default `smart`**.

- `smart` — a helper LLM assesses risk; low-risk commands auto-approved, genuinely dangerous auto-denied, uncertain cases escalated to manual

- `manual` — ask every time
- `off` — equivalent to `--yolo`

Timeout defaults to `300` seconds; **no reply means fail-closed**.

There is also an always-active hardline blocklist. It includes:

- `rm -rf /`
- fork bombs
- `dd` to block devices, etc.

Neither `--yolo` nor `approvals.mode: off` can bypass it.

There are also **user-editable deny rules**: `approvals.deny`.
They use fnmatch globs, case-insensitive.
You can write "yolo except these".

**② DM pairing (deny by default).** The authorization check runs in this order:

- platform allow-all
- **DM pairing approved list**
- platform allowlist (`TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS` etc.)
- global allowlist
- global allow-all
- **Default: deny**

The pairing flow uses an 8-digit code:

`hermes pairing approve <platform> <code>`
`unauthorized_dm_behavior` defaults to `pair`.
It can also be `ignore` / `decline`.
Pairing codes expire after 1 hour, are rate-limited, and 5 failures lock for 1 hour.

**③ Container isolation (off by default).** `terminal.backend` defaults to `local`.
Container isolation activates only when switching to specific backends:

- docker / ssh / singularity
- modal / daytona / vercel

When enabled, the official docs list a full set of Docker hardening flags:

- `--cap-drop ALL`
- `--security-opt no-new-privileges`
- `--pids-limit 256`
- noexec tmpfs, etc.

**The migration script touches secrets.** `hermes claw migrate` imports API keys from five services:

- Telegram
- OpenRouter / OpenAI
- Anthropic
- ElevenLabs

The official docs provide `--dry-run` preview.

⚠ **Unknown: gateway port security — the official docs have no dedicated section.**

The dashboard side has OAuth / self-hosted OIDC authentication.
axes.fit:
**Six scenarios it fits.**

- You want a **resident cross-platform personal assistant**
  (six platforms: Telegram / Discord / Slack / WhatsApp / Signal / Email)

- You want it on a cloud VM or serverless, not tied to your laptop
- You need scheduled tasks running unattended
- You need cross-session memory and self-accumulating skills
- You want a self-built endpoint or multi-provider setups like OpenRouter
- You need command-level approval and DM pairing as the security boundary

**Three scenarios it does not fit.**

- Coding-only work — it is a general assistant; coding is just one thing it does
- Using it as an embedded SDK — it is a full runtime, not a library
- You need detailed "state vs context" layering guarantees — it has many mechanisms,
  but the official docs do not organize them along those two layers

⚠ **Enterprise multi-user and auditing: the official docs provide no dedicated documentation.**

**Security and messaging pages checked**: they cover only single-owner
allowlist / DM pairing authorization, not multi-tenant auditing.

sections.选型第一提醒：它不是编程框架:
This is the single thing this page most needs to say up front.
**Hermes is not on the same layer as the other harnesses we list:**

| Object | Positioning | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| LangGraph / Google ADK / CrewAI | orchestration frameworks for coding tasks | Python code |
| Deep Agents | batteries-included harness for coding | Python code |
| OpenHands | self-hosted agent control center | Web UI |
| **Hermes Agent** | **a resident cross-platform personal assistant** | **TUI + six messaging platforms** |

Coding is just one thing Hermes can do.
The official description of it:

> "runs anywhere, not just your laptop"

The messaging entry points are six: **Telegram, Discord, Slack**,
**WhatsApp, Signal, Email**.
It can also connect to Home Assistant.

⚠ **One more piece of predecessor information we must record.** The README has a standalone
**"Migrating from OpenClaw"** section.
`hermes setup` auto-detects `~/.openclaw` and offers migration.

⚠ **Unknown: the relationship between Hermes and OpenClaw (same team? a rename?) is not verified by us.**
**We record only the README's first-party facts.**

sections.终端后端清单：这是它最独特的一格:
> README original (2026-10-23 rolling-verification edition):

> **terminal backends** — **local, Docker, SSH, Modal, Daytona, and Vercel Sandbox** —
> **plus plugin backends such as Singularity/Apptainer**.
> Daytona and Modal offer **serverless persistence** — your agent's environment
> **hibernates when idle and wakes on demand**, costing nearly nothing between sessions.

⚠ **Three things to make clear.**

**① These are terminal backends — meaning "where tools execute", not a deployment-method list.**
local runs on your machine, Docker is a container, SSH is a remote machine,
Modal/Daytona/Vercel are serverless.

**② The list itself changes.** When verified on 2026-10-01 the README said "Seven terminal backends" and listed
Singularity in the main list; on the 2026-10-23 rolling verification Singularity had moved to plugin backends
(such as Singularity/Apptainer), leaving six in the main list. Cite such lists with the verification date.

**③ "Hibernates when idle" is not the same as "always resident".**
The official word is hibernate; waking has latency.
State consistency during hibernation is not verified by us.

Compare [OpenHands](./openhands.md): it also leads with "the agent keeps running after you close the laptop".
The difference is that there it is an **optional deployment form**, while Hermes makes it the **default form**.

### Memory is plaintext markdown files (an important advantage)

From the migration list in the **"Migrating from OpenClaw"** section —
unusually concrete first-party file-level evidence:

| File / directory | Content |
|---|---|
| `SOUL.md` | persona file |
| `MEMORY.md`, `USER.md` | memory entries |
| `AGENTS.md` | workspace instructions |

**Memory is readable, diffable, hand-editable markdown** — not a black box inside a database.

There is also a separate **Context Files** concept.
(docs `features/context-files`) The official definition:

> "Project context that shapes **every** conversation"

i.e. project context files affect every conversation.

**Its format and precedence are verified**: first match wins.
`.hermes.md` → `AGENTS.override.md` → `AGENTS.md` → `CLAUDE.md` → `.cursorrules`.
**`SOUL.md` is always loaded separately as the identity file.** (see axes.local_files)
sections.权限：六个平台入口让「谁能指挥它」成为核心问题:
The README's docs directory has a standalone **Security** section, subtitle verbatim:

> **Command approval, DM pairing, container isolation**

**Item by item.**

**① Command approval — command-level approval.**
**Default `smart`**: a helper LLM assesses risk; low-risk auto-approved, dangerous auto-denied, uncertain escalated to manual.
Timeout `300` seconds, fail-closed.
There is also an always-active hardline blocklist, unaffected by those two switches.

Users can also write their own deny rules: `approvals.deny`.
They use fnmatch globs, case-insensitive.

**This is not on the same layer as other products' approaches.**

- OpenHands uses an API-key mechanism
- Codex SDK has four `ApprovalMode` values

**② DM pairing — private-chat pairing: only paired users can command it.**
**Deny by default**: in the authorization-check order, the pairing approved list sits before the platform allowlist.
If nothing matches, deny.
The pairing flow uses an 8-digit code:

- `hermes pairing approve <platform> <code>`

> **With six messaging entry points, this item is extremely important.**
> For an agent that takes instructions over Telegram / WhatsApp and acts on the file system,
> **"who can give it orders" is the most critical security question** — which is why we list it separately.

**③ Container isolation — off by default.**
`terminal.backend` defaults to `local`.
Isolation activates when switching to this backend group:

- docker / ssh
- singularity
- modal / daytona / vercel

The migration list covered by `hermes claw migrate` includes:

> **API keys** — allowlisted secrets (**Telegram, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs**)

This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested runs** (tailored to the general-assistant + resident form):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | **Default state of DM pairing and command approval** | the precondition of deployment safety, and our biggest gap |
| 2 | Actual information retention after `/compress` | our most-watched dimension, but compression is manually triggered |
| 3 | Wake latency and state consistency after Modal/Daytona hibernation | the official docs stress cost savings, but wake experience decides daily usability |
| 4 | One round with a local quantized model via a self-built endpoint | the README explicitly supports it; a combination our readers care about |
| 5 | How much subagent RPC's "zero context cost" actually saves | the official claim is unquantified |
| 6 | Cron task behavior after a gateway restart | the core reliability question for unattended scenarios |
| 7 | Using it for coding-only vs a dedicated coding framework | it positions itself as a general assistant; we owe an honest judgment |

related: **The same residency need, different form**: both lead with "the agent keeps running after you close the laptop". OpenHands is a control center with a Web UI plus scheduled/webhook triggers; this object is TUI + six messaging platforms + built-in cron, and positions itself as a general assistant rather than pure coding.
Same general-harness family, but Deep Agents targets coding tasks (filesystem + subagents are its selling points) while this object targets a resident cross-platform personal assistant.

**The memory-and-state dividing line**: LangGraph explicitly separates working memory from persistent memory, with checkpoints persisted every superstep; this object has richer mechanisms but the official docs don't split those two layers, and its memory is plaintext markdown files.
